paragraphs: I studied abroad at National Taiwan University in Taiwan for a total of two months in three departments: ophthalmology, endocrinology and family medicine. This time I was the only exchange student from Nagoya University to National Taiwan University, and I was full of anxiety, but through this study abroad I was able to have many valuable experiences. Although it is only a part, I would like to report what I experienced through the study abroad.

National Taiwan University is in Taipei, the largest city in Taiwan, in an urban area so central that one can walk to Taipei Station. The hospital is larger than Nagoya University Hospital, with three buildings, the obstetrics and gynecology and pediatrics building, an outpatient building and a ward building, and has over 2,300 beds. As for life in Taiwan, eating out is cheap, so I ate out most of the time. For getting around, within Taipei the subway is well developed and rental bicycles are also widespread, and I used them often. To go from Taipei to other cities one can travel by railway, high-speed rail and bus. The language is basically Chinese. I myself went abroad knowing no Chinese at all, but there were many people who can speak English and I had little trouble. However, when I studied Chinese and used a little, people were pleased.

I first studied in ophthalmology for two weeks. In ophthalmology, in the first week I joined a group of fifth-year students and studied together with them, and in the second week with sixth-year students, and in the spare time I observed operations. In the clerkship I did outpatient observation, watched video lectures, and experienced examinations using actual testing equipment. In the outpatient clinic, not only observing, I also took histories from actual patients and performed slit-lamp examinations together with the other students. The outpatient clinic and video lectures were basically in Chinese, but the local students translated into English for me, so I was able to understand. As for operations, I saw operations that are common in Japan too, such as cataract and glaucoma, vitrectomy for retinal detachment and epiretinal membrane, strabismus surgery and surgery for nasolacrimal duct obstruction. All the operations were almost the same as in Japan, and I felt that medicine is internationally standardized.

Next I studied in endocrinology for four weeks. In endocrinology I took part in the case conference twice a week, rounds, observation of thyroid ultrasound and so on. I did the rounds mainly together with other students and the residents. On the endocrinology ward, there happened to be an elderly woman who could speak a little Japanese, and I mainly did the rounds for this patient. This patient, in her 90s, had apparently learned Japanese during the Japanese rule of Taiwan, and I remember she was very pleased when I used Japanese. Thyroid ultrasound was performed about 50 times a day, and I was taught how to use the ultrasound and how to read the images.

The last, family medicine, I studied for two weeks together with other exchange students from Japan. In family medicine I was allowed to see the outpatient clinic, the palliative care ward and home visits. The family medicine outpatient clinic was divided into various kinds, such as a lifestyle disease clinic, a diabetes clinic and a travel medicine clinic. In particular, I had never seen a travel medicine clinic in Japan, so it was fresh. I was also allowed to observe a Taiwanese travel medicine conference. At that conference, people such as Taiwanese government officials were discussing the country's infectious disease control, and it was a valuable experience. The palliative care ward I had never seen in Japan and was very interesting. There were many volunteers on the ward, doing aromatherapy and bathing patients in baths that can be entered while lying down. I too actually did aromatherapy together with the volunteers. In home visits I was able to see actual Taiwanese homes. In Taiwan families can perform more procedures than in Japan, and I felt that home medical care is well developed.

As a big event outside the clerkships, I think taking part in the university-wide Taiwan-Japan language exchange club was significant. There, many Taiwanese students and Japanese exchange students belonged, and language exchange was done several times a month. I too learned Chinese there and was able to use it. They also held various other events, and I made many friends and went to various places and played with them. I am truly glad I took the plunge and joined.

Finally, I would like to express my gratitude to everyone at the International Collaboration Office who gave me this opportunity, the doctors who gave lectures, and everyone at National Taiwan University. Thank you very much.
